units.translation: 1035. μουνογενῆ: Hesiod (Theog. 426): 'nor, because she is an only child, has the goddess obtained less honor.' Musaeus (2 B 16 Diels-Kranz) relates that Zeus fell in love with Asteria and had intercourse with her, and after having intercourse gave her to Perses; from her Hecate was born to him. LmP

1085. ἔστι τις αἰπεινοῖσιν: that Thessaly is surrounded by mountains on all sides, Herodotus (VII 129) relates. Into it also other rivers flow, but especially four of the notable ones, Peneius, Apidanus, Pamisus, and Enipeus; when these mingle, the Peneius, prevailing by its name, makes the others nameless.
25 also the words εἰς αὐτὴν up to the end are taken from Herodotus

b. ἔνθα Προμηθεύς· that Deucalion was the son of Prometheus and Pandora, Hesiod says in the first book of the Catalogues (fg 2 Rz.²), and that Hellen was the son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, from whom the Hellenes and Hellas are named. That Deucalion ruled Thessaly, Hellanicus says in the first book of the Deucalioneia (4 fg 6 ab J.). That Deucalion also founded an altar of the twelve gods, Hellanicus says in the same work.
